title: Stein Variational Distributional Reinforcement Learning: Score-Guided Particles for Multivariate Return Distributions

paper.title: Stein Variational Distributional Reinforcement Learning: Score-Guided Particles for Multivariate Return Distributions
paper.abstract:
Abstract Decisions that weigh several reward signals against each other require the joint distribution of the return vector. Categorical critics scale exponentially in the reward dimension, and quantiles have no canonical multivariate analogue. Multivariate distributional critics therefore represent each return distribution by M M equal-weight particles trained with a discrepancy loss.
Beyond their atoms, the particles provide no sampler and cannot resolve events rarer than 1 / M 1/M . We propose Stein variational distributional RL (SVDRL). Its critic outputs Stein particles, which Stein variational gradient descent transports along a learned score field of the distributional Bellman target. We learn this field by bootstrapped denoising score matching across noise levels and tie it across the Bellman recursion by a consistency loss, which we prove is a non-expansive temporal-difference scheme in score space. The same field certifies the particles. Its reverse-diffusion sampler satisfies a supremal Wasserstein policy-evaluation bound that holds for bounded, possibly multimodal returns. The Stein particles inherit this bound up to a gap that we measure without ground truth, and the sampler answers tail-risk queries below the particle resolution at any sample size. Empirically, SVDRL is more accurate on rare events than particle critics with the same number of particles, and on par on MuJoCo continuous control.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Distributional reinforcement learning models the distribution of the return rather than only its expectation ( Bellemare et al.,, 2017 ) . With multivariate rewards, risk- and correlation-sensitive decisions depend on the joint distribution of the return components ( Zhang et al.,, 2021 ; Hayes et al.,, 2022 ) . The univariate representations do not carry over: categorical grids ( Bellemare et al.,, 2017 ) need 𝒪 ⁡ ( M d ) \mathcal{O}(M^{d}) atoms, and quantiles ( Dabney et al., 2018a, ; Dabney et al., 2018b, ) have no canonical analogue for d > 1 d>1 . Existing multivariate methods therefore represent the return distribution by M M particles trained with a discrepancy loss, e.g., MMD ( Zhang et al.,, 2021 ) , Sinkhorn divergences ( Sun et al.,, 2024 ) , or sliced divergences ( Debes and Tuytelaars, 2026b, ) . The theory of these methods covers the Bellman operator, which contracts in the respective supremal divergence, but not the learned particles. We show that this gap is structural. Equal-weight particles carry no density and no sampler, and M M of them cannot represent an event of probability below 1 / M 1/M , whatever loss trains them ( Propositions 1 and 1 ). We instead learn the return score field , the smoothed score of the return distribution at all noise levels. Smoothing commutes with the Bellman update up to a rescaling of the noise level ( Lemma 1 ), so the field satisfies its own Bellman equation, and we learn it along a noise schedule ( Song and Ermon,, 2019 ) by bootstrapped denoising score matching ( Lemma 4 ) and by temporal differences in score space ( Theorem 2 ). A single noise level does not suffice, as it cannot certify mode masses ( Remark 2 ). We sample from the field by reverse diffusion. For fast action selection we additionally keep M M particles per state–action pair, the Stein particles, which we transport along the field by Stein variational gradient descent (SVGD) ( Liu and Wang,, 2016 ) and amortize into a critic. The training risk controls the sampled return distribution in total variation and w 1 w_{1} for bounded multimodal returns, where log-concavity and related assumptions fail ( Theorem 3 ). This yields a policy-evaluation bound in w ¯ 1 \bar{w}_{1} ( Theorem 4 ), certified mode masses ( Corollaries 6 and 8 ), and a CVaR estimate whose error does not depend on M M ( Theorem 6 ). No single critic is accurate on every return law, and we show which error limits each family. Equal-weight particles suffer from a resolution floor : they round event probabilities and mixture weights to multiples of 1 / M 1/M ( Proposition 1 ). A score field suffers from smoothing bias and is hard to learn where the return law is atomic or its modes lie far apart relative to their widths ( Propositions 2 and 2 ). SVDRL keeps both objects, and a hybrid rule reports, per state–action pair and without ground truth, the Stein particles on separated or atomic clusters and the sampler draws elsewhere ( Definitions 1 and 1 ). SVDRL is, to our knowledge, the first certified multivariate score-based critic for possibly multimodal returns, and its Stein particles inherit the certificate up to a gap measured without ground truth ( Theorem 4 ). At equal particle count, SVDRL is more accurate than the best particle critic in every rare-event comparison ( Section 5 ). On all eight synthetic MDPs the hybrid wins within-mode shape against the competitors as specified, although at matched compute they win the unimodal ones. The competitors’ own benchmarks place the boundary at atomic laws, and on MuJoCo SAC-SVDRL is on par in return and has the most accurate critic distribution on three of four. Its stratified Bellman target set and running-mean moment matching improve every particle critic we tested. Figure 1: A rare event below the particle resolution. Schematic. A catastrophe of mass p < 1 / M p<1/M needs a fraction of a particle, so particle critics round its probability to a multiple of 1 / M 1/M ( Proposition 1 ). SVDRL learns a density, which carries any mass; on the rare-event chain it estimates p = 0.005 p=0.005 far better than particle critics with M = 128 M=128 ( Sections 5 and 5 ).

sections.heading: 3 Stein Variational Distributional RL
sections.text: We model the return distribution function through its smoothed score over all noise levels, the return score field , and use the Stein particles only to represent it. The smoothed score exists for every return law, and smoothing commutes with the affine bootstrap map up to a rescaling of the noise level ( Lemma 1 ), which yields a Bellman equation in score space ( Corollary 1 ).

sections.heading: The Resample-Move Update.
sections.text: In the tabular experiments SVDRL keeps M M particles per state–action pair and updates them by a resample-move step of sequential Monte Carlo ( Gilks and Berzuini,, 2001 ) in four steps ( Algorithm 1 ). (ii) Resampling replaces a fraction ρ \rho of the particles by targets; ρ = 1 \rho=1 carries the branch masses exactly up to 1 / M 1/M . The (iii) Stein move runs SVGD along s ψ s_{\psi} down the levels σ ℓ ≤ σ start \sigma_{\ell}\leq\sigma_{\mathrm{start}} with relaxation α \alpha , and (iv) moment matching maps the cloud affinely onto the target set’s moments. sections.heading: The Sampler and the Hybrid Rule.
sections.text: The sampler draws from the field by reverse diffusion of the EMA networks ( Definition 2 ); one set of N ≫ M N\gg M draws answers CVaR of any scalarization, event probabilities and conditional queries ( Corollaries 10 and 11 ). Lemma 2 says the field is learnable when the return law has a density whose components are not far apart relative to their widths; we turn it into a rule that the agent evaluates on its own particles, without ground truth, with a threshold fixed in advance ( Appendix B ). Definition 1 (Hybrid rule) . Let r r be the ratio of the smallest gap between single-linkage clusters of the particle cloud at ( x , a ) (x,a) to the largest within-cluster standard deviation, after merging particles closer than the field’s smallest noise level. The hybrid rule reports the particles if r > 6 r>6 , or if a cluster of at least two particles is narrower than the field’s smallest noise level; otherwise it reports the sampler draws.

sections.heading: SAC-SVDRL.
sections.text: In continuous control SVDRL is the critic of SAC ( Haarnoja et al.,, 2018 ) : an amortized critic outputs M M particles regressed onto the transported cloud, i.e., amortized SVGD ( Feng et al.,, 2017 ) , and a moment head sets the score network’s standardization and moment-matching target ( Appendix B ).

sections.heading: Protocol.
sections.text: In the tabular experiments a seed’s error is its mean over the last 20 % 20\,\% of training, which averages out the fluctuation of single evaluations. Configurations are selected on tuning seeds and reported on different seeds that the selection did not use, in the rare-event study additionally on a second set of fresh seeds. We report the interquartile mean (IQM) or median over seeds with 95 % 95\,\% bootstrap intervals; on the synthetic MDPs and the chain a comparison is a win or a loss when the Welch t t statistic is at most − 2 -2 or at least 2 2 , and in the rare-event study it compares IQM errors ( Appendix C ). The particle competitors are MMD critics ( Nguyen-Tang et al.,, 2021 ; Zhang et al.,, 2021 ) with RBF, MD3QN and energy kernels, sliced Cramér and sliced w 2 w_{2} critics, the persistent-particle objectives of Debes and Tuytelaars, 2026b () and Sinkhorn critics ( Sun et al.,, 2024 ) , each with a tuned learning rate and each also run with our stratified target set ( Section B.1 ). The MMD critic with the energy kernel, energy MMD, is our own variant; its loss is the energy distance, in which the multivariate distributional Bellman operator contracts ( Wiltzer et al.,, 2024 ) . Below 1 / M 1/M , particle critics with M = 128 M=128 miss the catastrophe and SVDRL’s sampler errs an order of magnitude less; sliced w 2 w_{2} needs M = 2048 M=2048 to locate it. sections.heading: Rare Events.
sections.text: In the rare-event chain ( Appendix C ) the risky root action leads, D ∈ { 0 , 2 } D\in\{0,2\} steps later, to a catastrophe of mass p ∈ { 0.002 , 0.005 , 0.01 } p\in\{0.002,0.005,0.01\} in a two-dimensional return, and the queries on the joint law are CVaR down to α = 0.001 \alpha=0.001 , event probabilities, chance constraints, conditional tails and entropic risk. Six particle critics answer from their particles or from a kernel density estimate on them, a quantile critic is trained on the oracle scalarization, and SVDRL bootstraps from moment-matched sampler draws ( Theorem 4 (ii), Remark 5 ) and answers with N = 10 5 N=10^{5} draws. At equal particle count, M = 128 M=128 , SVDRL has a lower IQM error than the best particle critic in 60 of 60 rare-event and 12 of 12 bulk comparisons, and on fresh seeds its error is lower by a median factor of 5.0 on rare events and 3.9 on the bulk ( Figure 2 ). At comparable compute, against particle critics with M = 512 M=512 , it is still more accurate in 40 of 60 rare-event and 10 of 12 bulk comparisons. At p = 0.005 p=0.005 and D = 2 D=2 it is more accurate than every particle critic on every query of Table 5 , from their atoms or from a kernel density estimate, and the quantile critic on the oracle scalarization matches it only at CVaR 0.01 of that scalarization. Its | log ⁡ P ^ / P | |\log\hat{P}/P| there is 0.16, against 4.8 to 8.5 for the particle critics. Particle critics need about 10 / p 10/p particles to locate the catastrophe: with M = 2048 M=2048 , sliced w 2 w_{2} reaches a CVaR 0.001 error of 0.30 against SVDRL’s 6.9. Even then SVDRL is more accurate on the mass ( | log ⁡ P ^ / P | |\log\hat{P}/P| 0.16 against 0.26), on the chance-constrained decisions (accuracy 1.00 against 0.96) and on the bulk (CVaR 0.1 error 0.94 against 1.5). With sampler bootstrapping the catastrophe survives the recursion even at M = 32 M=32 for p ≥ 0.005 p\geq 0.005 , where every particle critic loses it ( Section D.1 ). This requires the rare mode to have a density. Resource gathering from MO-Gymnasium ( Felten et al.,, 2023 ) has atomic returns, with death as the rare event. At the standard attack probability p = 0.1 p=0.1 and at p = 0.02 {p=0.02} , SVDRL’s particles ( M = 128 M=128 ) are the best critic: their | log ⁡ P ^ / P | |\log\hat{P}/P| for death is 0.028 and 0.15 against at best 0.19 and 0.45, their chance-constrained choice is wrong in 0 and 13 % of the cases against 14 and 41 %, and their CVaR error at p = 0.1 p=0.1 is 0.0035 against 0.030 (medians over ten seeds, Section D.4 ). The stratified target set holds each atom at its mass up to 1 / M 1/M , and at p = 0.005 < 1 / M p=0.005<1/M full replacement rounds the mass without bias: the time-averaged estimate is 0.0053 for P = 0.005 P=0.005 . The sampler fails on these atomic laws, as Lemma 2 predicts, and the hybrid rule matches the particles on the probability of death and on the chance-constrained choice.

sections.heading: Chain with Reward Noise.
sections.text: The chain of Debes and Tuytelaars, 2026b () has ten reward dimensions, to which we add Gaussian reward noise of scale σ r \sigma_{r} . On the atomic chain, σ r = 0 \sigma_{r}=0 , their persistent particles win, as Lemma 2 predicts. With reward noise, σ r ≥ 0.05 \sigma_{r}\geq 0.05 , and against their critics at their published settings with M = 128 M=128 instead of 500 500 particles, SVDRL’s moment-matched sampler ( 4096 4096 draws) wins every shape metric and the mean ( Figure 3 ), e.g., with 0.15 times the best competitor’s energy distance and 0.56 times its mean error at σ r = 0.2 \sigma_{r}=0.2 . With more particles they win shape at matched compute: with M = 4096 M=4096 their shape errors are 1.6 to 3.0 times lower than the sampler’s. Our stratified target set lowers the energy distance and mean error of every one of their variants, and running-mean moment matching, a shift of their particles to a running mean of the bootstrap targets, lets them win the mean too, so both of our components transfer to their critics ( Section D.3 ).

sections.heading: Continuous Control.
sections.text: On four MuJoCo environments ( Towers et al.,, 2024 ) , SAC with the SVDRL critic runs against SAC and against IQN, MD3QN and energy MMD critics on the same trunk ( Table 3 ). Its return is on par with SAC’s, with overlapping 95 % 95\,\% intervals on all four environments, although its IQM on HalfCheetah is lower. Its critic distribution is the most accurate on three of four: its centered w 2 w_{2} , which removes the twin-critic bias of the means, is the lowest on HalfCheetah, Walker2d and Hopper, with the interval entirely below IQN’s, and second on Ant, behind energy MMD. With the default configuration of HalfCheetah it is 0.70 on Walker2d and 0.57 on Ant ( Table 18 ), the same ranks.

sections.heading: Multivariate Distributional RL.
sections.text: MD3QN ( Zhang et al.,, 2021 ) trains particles with an MMD loss, SinkhornDRL ( Sun et al.,, 2024 ) with entropic optimal transport, and sliced DRL ( Debes and Tuytelaars, 2026b, ) with sliced divergences, whose max-sliced version also contracts under matrix discounting. Their analyses establish the contraction of the Bellman operator in the respective divergence, and Wiltzer et al., (2024) prove convergence of categorical dynamic programming and TD learning on a fixed support; our guarantees concern a learned score-based representation of possibly multimodal returns ( Theorems 3 and 4 ), also under matrix discounting ( Corollary 9 ). Yoo et al., (2026) extend quantile regression to vector returns through the Knothe–Rosenblatt map.

sections.heading: Generative Critics.
sections.text: Diffusion and flow critics such as VDRL ( Hu et al.,, 2025 ) , DBC ( Ding et al.,, 2026 ) , Value Flows ( Dong et al.,, 2026 ) and FlowIQN ( Groom et al.,, 2026 ) model scalar returns, and DBC and FlowIQN rely on one-dimensional structure, inverse distribution functions or sorted couplings. Bellman Diffusion ( Li et al.,, 2024 ) learns unnormalized density fields of scalar returns on which the Bellman operator acts linearly, and Corollary 1 is the normalized counterpart in score space, which is nonlinear through the posterior branch weights. The Bellman GAN ( Freirich et al.,, 2019 ) samples vector-valued returns and distributional Sobolev training ( Debes and Tuytelaars, 2026a, ) returns with their action gradients, without a density or a score. None of these works bounds the error of a learned multivariate representation.

sections.heading: Particle Transport.
sections.text: SVGD ( Liu and Wang,, 2016 ) is a kernelized Wasserstein gradient flow of the KL divergence ( Liu,, 2017 ; Chewi et al.,, 2020 ) , and its convergence guarantees rest on functional inequalities of the target, with constants that grow exponentially with the separation of modes ( Proposition 3 (i)). In RL, SVGD has so far trained policies ( Liu et al.,, 2017 ; Messaoud et al.,, 2024 ) , not return distributions.

sections.heading: 7 Limitations and Conclusion
sections.text: The main errors of Table 1 also mark where SVDRL is not the best critic. The sampler fails on atomic and widely separated laws, such as the atomic chain, resource gathering and the far modes of MDP4, as Lemma 2 predicts, and the hybrid rule reports the particles there. A light rare mode far from the bulk comes out too wide ( Figure 5 ), and a static fit of the score network to draws of the true law reproduces this, with 13 to 15 times the true width ( Appendix E ). At equal N N the sampler loses to fitted particle clouds ( Section 5 ). In SAC-SVDRL a linear-variance floor made one Ant seed diverge, which a log-variance head removes on HalfCheetah and a standardized moment head limits on multi-objective MuJoCo. SVDRL learns a Bellman-consistent score field that yields a certified sampler without a resolution floor and Stein particles. It answers rare-event queries that particles cannot represent, and two of its components improve every particle critic we tested. At equal particle count it is more accurate than the best particle critic in 60 of 60 rare-event comparisons, and in continuous control SAC-SVDRL learns the most accurate critic distribution on three of four MuJoCo environments.

sections.heading: AI Use Statement
sections.text: In this work, we used generative AI tools for the following tasks. It was used to optimize the original implementation of the methods by the authors to improve performance and experimental throughput. All generated code was reviewed by the authors, compared numerically against the original implementation and an extensive set of unit tests. We further used these tools during the writing process as follows. Drafting of sections, typesetting the proofs by the authors into their final form, and grammar checks. The final form of the proofs was checked manually by the authors to ensure they remained consistent. Whenever a tool suggested the addition of a reference in any of the sections, it was flagged and manually checked for correctness by the authors. To ensure that results could not inadvertently be changed by the tool during typesetting, all are generated automatically from the logged experimental data. Any error in the proofs as well as incorrect attribution of theoretical or empirical results is therefore due to the authors and we take full responsibility for it and everything written in the paper. sections.heading: Appendix B Method Details
sections.text: This section completes Section 3 with the details that reproduce the reported runs. The tabular variant runs on the synthetic MDPs, the rare-event chain, the chain of Debes and Tuytelaars, 2026b () and resource gathering, and SAC-SVDRL on MuJoCo; Section B.1 lists every setting.

sections.heading: Stratified Bellman Target Set.
sections.text: The M M successors of an update are drawn by systematic resampling ( Kitagawa,, 1996 ) , so a branch of probability p p receives ⌊ M ​ p ⌋ \lfloor Mp\rfloor or ⌈ M ​ p ⌉ \lceil Mp\rceil targets. Within the block of n k n_{k} draws of one successor, the standard normal reward noise is a Latin hypercube sample ( McKay et al.,, 1979 ) : each coordinate takes each of the n k n_{k} equal-probability strata of 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , 1 ) \mathcal{N}(0,1) exactly once, at a uniform position within the stratum, with the strata permuted independently per coordinate. Each draw is still marginally a successor and reward of the model, so the targets stay unbiased, while their empirical law matches the branch masses up to 1 / M 1/M and spreads the noise evenly over the quantiles of each coordinate. The successor particle of a draw is one of the current particles at the successor pair.

sections.heading: Resample-Move Update.
sections.text: Each update replaces round ⁡ ( ρ ​ M ) \mathrm{round}(\rho M) particles by targets and runs the Stein move on the cloud ( Algorithm 1 ). The relaxation z ← z + α ⁡ ( z ~ − z ) z\leftarrow z+\alpha(\tilde{z}-z) then moves the cloud toward the transported cloud z ~ \tilde{z} . The annealing schedule has ten geometric levels σ ℓ \sigma_{\ell} from 5 5 to 0.1 0.1 in PopArt-normalized units, and the Stein move takes T ℓ = 10 T_{\ell}=10 SVGD steps at every level σ ℓ ≤ σ start \sigma_{\ell}\leq\sigma_{\mathrm{start}} . The SVGD direction uses the RBF kernel with the bandwidth recomputed at every step, h ℓ = clip ⁡ ( h med , 0.1 ​ σ ℓ , 2 ​ σ ℓ ) h_{\ell}=\mathrm{clip}(h_{\mathrm{med}},0.1\,\sigma_{\ell},2\,\sigma_{\ell}) , where h med 2 h_{\mathrm{med}}^{2} is the median of the squared pairwise distances divided by 2 ​ log ⁡ ( M + 1 ) 2\log(M+1) , so that a balanced bimodal cloud at a low level keeps h ℓ h_{\ell} of the order of σ ℓ \sigma_{\ell} and not of the mode separation. The steps are preconditioned by Adam ( Kingma and Ba,, 2015 ) , with step size 0.1 0.1 and a state per particle and coordinate that is carried across the levels of one update and reset at the next, and every step is followed by the coordinatewise projection onto the return box B R B_{R} . The single configuration replaces the whole cloud, ρ = 1 \rho=1 , with α = 0.001 \alpha=0.001 and σ start = 1 \sigma_{\mathrm{start}}=1 ; it is the selected configuration on MDP2, MDP3, MDP4, MDP6 and MDP7. On MDP1 the selected configuration uses α = 0.1 \alpha=0.1 , and on the unimodal MDP5 and MDP8 it transports the previous cloud through the whole schedule toward the stratified target set, ρ = 0 \rho=0 and α = 1 \alpha=1 .

sections.heading: Moment Matching.
sections.text: After the Stein move the cloud is mapped affinely onto the moments of the target set and projected onto B R B_{R} , z i ← proj B R ​ ( m y + ( z i − z ¯ ) ⊙ s y / s z ) z_{i}\leftarrow\mathrm{proj}_{B_{R}}\big(m_{y}+(z_{i}-\bar{z})\odot s_{y}/s_{z}\big) , with the per-dimension means m y , z ¯ m_{y},\bar{z} and standard deviations s y , s z s_{y},s_{z} of the targets and of the cloud; on MDP8 the map matches the full covariance instead. It corrects the spread, since SVGD with finitely many particles underestimates the variance of its target, increasingly so in higher dimensions ( Ba et al.,, 2022 ) , and on a self-looping state–action pair the bootstrap compounds a per-update variance bias by the factor 1 / ( 1 − γ 2 ) 1/(1-\gamma^{2}) , as in Remark 5 . Sampler bootstrapping applies the same map to the sampler draws. On the chain the draws are instead shifted, at evaluation only, to a running mean of the bootstrap targets at ( x , a ) (x,a) , an exponential average with weight max ⁡ ( 1 / 128 , 1 / t ) \max(1/128,1/t) at update t t ; we call this running-mean moment matching, and given to the competitors’ particles it is the second of the two components that transfer ( Section D.3 ).

sections.heading: Score Network.
sections.text: The tabular variant keeps one score network per state–action pair, an MLP with three hidden layers of 128 128 Swish units in the energy parameterization E ψ ​ ( z , σ ) = c out ​ f ψ ​ ( c in ​ z , c noise ) − ‖ z ‖ 2 / ( 2 ​ ( σ 2 + σ d 2 ) ) E_{\psi}(z,\sigma)=c_{\mathrm{out}}f_{\psi}(c_{\mathrm{in}}z,c_{\mathrm{noise}})-\|z\|^{2}/(2(\sigma^{2}+\sigma_{\mathrm{d}}^{2})) with the EDM scalings ( Karras et al.,, 2022 ) , whose score is s ψ = ∇ z E ψ s_{\psi}=\nabla_{z}E_{\psi} and whose noise level enters every hidden layer by feature-wise affine modulation (FiLM); the prior term makes the score grow linearly in z z , and Remark 3 applies Theorem 3 to it. It reads its input in standardized coordinates u = ( z − m ) / s u=(z-m)/s , where m m is the mean of the bootstrap targets at ( x , a ) (x,a) and s s one scale for all dimensions, the largest standard deviation of the targets, both exponential averages with weight 0.02 0.02 on the new value; the EDM scalings assume σ d ≈ 1 \sigma_{\mathrm{d}}\approx 1 , which holds only after this standardization. Each Bellman step takes two Adam steps (learning rate 10 − 3 10^{-3} ) on a batch of 256 256 samples of the DSM loss ( 4 ) and the consistency loss ( 5 ) with λ cons = 1 \lambda_{\mathrm{cons}}=1 and the weight λ ⁡ ( σ ) = σ 2 \lambda(\sigma)=\sigma^{2} , each sample with its own noise level, drawn log-uniformly from [ 0.002 , 80 ] [0.002,80] in standardized units. The target of ( 5 ) is the EMA network of the successor pair, and the online network under a stop-gradient where the successor is the pair being updated. The level grid of Theorem 2 , with ratio γ 1 / m \gamma^{1/m} , is a device of the analysis; the network is conditioned on a continuous noise level.

sections.heading: PopArt and the Return Box.
sections.text: Returns are normalized per reward dimension by PopArt, with exponential averages of weight 3 ⋅ 10 − 4 3\cdot 10^{-4} , a scale floor, and an output correction that preserves the predictions. A normalized return y ^ = ( y − m ) / s \hat{y}=(y-m)/s satisfies y ^ = r ^ + γ ​ z ^ \hat{y}=\hat{r}+\gamma\hat{z} with r ^ = ( r − ( 1 − γ ) ​ m ) / s \hat{r}=(r-(1-\gamma)m)/s , the same affine bootstrap with the same γ \gamma , so Lemma 1 and ( 5 ) hold verbatim in normalized space, which a nonlinear transform such as symlog would break. The return box B R B_{R} has the half-width r max / ( 1 − γ ) r_{\max}/(1-\gamma) per reward dimension; in the tabular variant r max = max c ⁡ ( | m c | + 5 ​ s c ) r_{\max}=\max_{c}(|m_{c}|+5s_{c}) over the reward channels c c with mean m c m_{c} and standard deviation s c s_{c} , and in SAC-SVDRL it is the running maximum of the absolute soft reward, which keeps the soft bootstrap inside B R B_{R} .

sections.heading: Sampler and Estimators.
sections.text: The sampler is the reverse diffusion of Definition 2 on the EMA score network ( Algorithm 2 ). On the synthetic MDPs and resource gathering it takes Euler steps on 512 512 geometric levels from σ u = 80 \sigma_{u}=80 to 0.002 0.002 in standardized units and returns N = 4096 N=4096 draws. In the rare-event study SVDRL bootstraps from moment-matched draws of its EMA sampler, 4 ​ M 4M per target set, and answers every query with N = 10 5 N=10^{5} draws. On the chain the sampler takes 256 256 Euler steps with a projection onto B R B_{R} at every step, its mean is matched to a debiased exponential average (weight 1 / 128 1/128 ) of the target means, and it returns 4096 4096 or 128 128 draws. Event probabilities, CVaR and decisions are read from the draws by plug-in, and conditional queries by rejection ( Corollary 11 ). sections.heading: Hybrid Rule.
sections.text: The rule of Definition 1 runs on the particles at ( x , a ) (x,a) without ground truth. First, particles closer than the field’s smallest noise level are merged, i.e., connected components of the graph with an edge whenever ‖ ( z i − z j ) / ε ‖ < 1 \|(z_{i}-z_{j})/\varepsilon\|<1 , with ε \varepsilon the smallest noise level in return units per dimension, each component replaced by its mean. Single-linkage clusters are then found top-down on the Euclidean minimum spanning tree of the merged points: a cluster is split at its longest edge whenever that edge exceeds three times the larger standard deviation of its two sides, the standard deviation being the square root of the largest eigenvalue of the count-weighted covariance. The ratio r r is the shortest accepted cut over the largest within-cluster standard deviation, and r = 0 r=0 for a single cluster. The rule reports the particles if r > 6 r>6 or if a cluster of at least two particles has a per-dimension standard deviation below ε \varepsilon in every dimension, and the sampler draws otherwise. The threshold 6 6 was fixed in advance, and the thresholds 4 4 and 10 10 were evaluated on tuning seeds only. The second clause was added after resource gathering exposed atoms of coincident particles, and it changes no entry of Table 2 .

sections.heading: SAC-SVDRL.
sections.text: SAC-SVDRL uses two distributional critics with M M particles each and a score network per critic, all four networks with EMA targets. The bootstrap targets use the rank-wise minimum of the two target critics’ sorted particles, with the soft reward r − γ ​ α ​ log ⁡ π ⁡ ( a ′ ∣ x ′ ) r-\gamma\alpha\log\pi(a^{\prime}\mid x^{\prime}) and one-step targets. A moment head regressed onto the mean and the central second moment of the bootstrap targets sets the standardization of the score network, which is conditioned on ( σ , x , a ) (\sigma,x,a) by FiLM, and the moment-matching target; the noise levels and the SVGD step are scaled by its predicted standard deviation, so that the annealing acts on a law of unit spread. The Stein move takes T ℓ = 2 T_{\ell}=2 steps at each of the ten levels, and each critic is regressed onto its transported cloud by matching ranks, L critic ​ ( θ ) = ∑ i ‖ z ( i ) θ ​ ( x , a ) − sg ⁡ [ z ( i ) SVGD ​ ( x , a ) ] ‖ 2 , L_{\mathrm{critic}}(\theta)=\textstyle\sum_{i}\big\|z_{(i)}^{\theta}(x,a)-\mathrm{sg}\!\left[z_{(i)}^{\mathrm{SVGD}}(x,a)\right]\big\|^{2}, (20) where z ( i ) z_{(i)} is the i i -th smallest particle of the one-dimensional return, which is the w 2 w_{2} -optimal matching in d = 1 d=1 . For a single Euler step of the transport the gradient of ( 20 ) is, by the chain rule, − 2 ε ∑ i J i ⊤ ϕ ^ ∗ ( z i θ ) -2\varepsilon\sum_{i}J_{i}^{\top}\hat{\phi}^{*}(z_{i}^{\theta}) with the Jacobians J i J_{i} of the critic’s particles, the direction of amortized SVGD ( Feng et al.,, 2017 ) . The policy minimizes 𝔼 x [ 𝔼 a ∼ π ( ⋅ | x ) [ α log π ( a | x ) − Q ( x , a ) ] ] \mathds{E}_{x}\left[\mathds{E}_{a\sim\pi(\cdot|x)}\left[\alpha\log\pi(a|x)-Q(x,a)\right]\right] with Q Q the smaller of the two critics’ particle means, the entropy coefficient α \alpha is adapted as in SAC, and every head uses the same running observation normalization. HalfCheetah uses this default configuration; on Walker2d, Hopper and Ant moment matching takes its mean from the bootstrap targets of the sampled transitions instead of the moment head, which gives the critic the temporal-difference signal directly. A variant with a log-variance moment head removes the floor of the linear variance head that made one Ant seed diverge ( Section D.5 ).

sections.heading: Appendix C Protocols
sections.text: This section specifies the environments, the statistics and the metrics of Section 5 , and the measured compute. Gymnasium and MO-Gymnasium are released under the MIT license and MuJoCo under the Apache 2.0 license; we reimplement the chain of Debes and Tuytelaars, 2026b () and the maze of Zhang et al., (2021) from their published definitions.

sections.heading: Synthetic MDPs.
sections.text: All synthetic MDPs have γ = 0.95 \gamma=0.95 and Gaussian rewards, deterministic at the root states, so their return laws are Gaussian mixtures. MDP1 has a single absorbing state with reward 𝒩 ⁡ ( 1 , 0.5 2 ) \mathcal{N}(1,0.5^{2}) . In MDP2 the root has reward 0 0 and branches with probabilities 0.3 0.3 and 0.7 0.7 into absorbing states with rewards 𝒩 ⁡ ( 1 , 0.3 2 ) \mathcal{N}(1,0.3^{2}) and 𝒩 ⁡ ( 2 , 0.4 2 ) \mathcal{N}(2,0.4^{2}) . MDP3 is two-dimensional with three modes, reached from the root with probabilities 0.4 0.4 , 0.35 0.35 and 0.25 0.25 . MDP4 is five-dimensional with three modes reached with the same probabilities, whose mean rewards are 3 3 times standard normal draws and whose covariances have eigenvalues drawn uniformly from [ 0.05 , 0.5 ] [0.05,0.5] in a random orthonormal basis, all drawn with the fixed random key 42 42 , which is part of the specification; the dimension sweep builds the MDP4 family in the same way for d ∈ { 2 , 3 , 5 , 8 , 10 } d\in\{2,3,5,8,10\} . MDP5 to MDP8 have one decision state whose actions lead to absorbing reward channels with i.i.d. Gaussian rewards from t = 0 t=0 on, so each channel’s return is Gaussian with 1 / ( 1 − γ ) 1/(1-\gamma) times the mean and 1 / ( 1 − γ 2 ) 1/(1-\gamma^{2}) times the covariance of its reward. MDP5 ( d = 2 d=2 ) has four deterministic actions with mean rewards ( 3 , 0.5 ) (3,0.5) , ( 2 , 2 ) (2,2) , ( 0.5 , 3 ) (0.5,3) and the dominated ( 1 , 1 ) (1,1) , all with covariance 0.04 ​ 𝐈 0.04\,\mathbf{I} . MDP6 ( d = 2 d=2 ) has a safe action with mean reward ( 2 , 1 ) (2,1) , a risky action that reaches ( 4 , 0.8 ) (4,0.8) or ( 0.2 , 1 ) (0.2,1) with probability 1 2 \frac{1}{2} each and variance 0.09 0.09 in the first objective, and an action with ( 0.5 , 3 ) (0.5,3) ; all other variances are 0.04 0.04 . MDP7 ( d = 3 d=3 ) has five deterministic actions with mean rewards ( 3 , 0.5 , 0.5 ) (3,0.5,0.5) , ( 0.5 , 3 , 0.5 ) (0.5,3,0.5) , ( 0.5 , 0.5 , 3 ) (0.5,0.5,3) , ( 2 , 2 , 0.3 ) (2,2,0.3) and ( 0.3 , 2 , 2 ) (0.3,2,2) and full covariances, with diagonal entries 0.03 0.03 to 0.06 0.06 and correlations of both signs. MDP8 ( d = 2 d=2 ) has two actions with the same mean reward ( 2 , 2 ) (2,2) and the covariances ( 0.5 ∓ 0.45 ∓ 0.45 0.5 ) \begin{pmatrix}0.5&\mp 0.45\\ \mp 0.45&0.5\end{pmatrix} , hedged and concentrated, and a low-variance action with mean reward ( 0.5 , 3 ) (0.5,3) and covariance 0.04 ​ 𝐈 0.04\,\mathbf{I} . The multimodal evaluated state–action pairs are those of MDP2, MDP3, MDP4 and MDP6. Every run takes 8000 8000 Bellman steps on MDP1 and MDP2 and 16 000 16\,000 on the other MDPs, with an evaluation every 800 800 steps up to 80 % 80\,\% of training and every 100 100 steps afterwards.

sections.heading: Choice of the Synthetic MDPs.
sections.text: Each MDP probes one property of the return law on which the critic families of Table 1 differ, and every return law is a Gaussian mixture, so every error is measured against the exact law. MDP1 and MDP2 are one-dimensional. MDP1 bootstraps through a self-loop, where any per-update bias in the spread of the cloud is amplified by the factor 1 / ( 1 − γ 2 ) 1/(1-\gamma^{2}) , and MDP2 has two modes with unequal masses and widths. MDP3 and MDP4 have three separated modes in two and five dimensions, with masses 0.4 0.4 , 0.35 0.35 and 0.25 0.25 , which M = 64 ​ d M=64d particles hold exactly only at d = 5 d=5 and d = 10 d=10 , so the MDP4 family separates the resolution floor of Proposition 1 from the growth of the error with the dimension. MDP5 to MDP8 have one decision state each and differ in what separates its actions. In MDP5 three Pareto-optimal actions and a dominated one differ only in their means, the baseline for decisions. In MDP6 a safe and a risky action have almost the same mean, ( 2 , 1 ) (2,1) against ( 2.1 , 0.9 ) (2.1,0.9) , and differ in their tails. MDP7 has correlated objectives in three dimensions. In MDP8 two actions have the same mean and the same marginals and differ only in the sign of the correlation, which no model of the per-dimension marginals can resolve. Together the eight MDPs cover unimodal laws, on which the within-mode shape decides (MDP1, MDP5, MDP7 and MDP8), and separated modes, on which the mode masses decide (MDP2, MDP3, MDP4 and MDP6), in one to five dimensions and up to ten in the dimension sweep. Gaussian rewards make the returns unbounded, so Assumption 1 holds for the synthetic MDPs only up to a truncation. The return box of Appendix B keeps every channel’s return within 5 ​ ( ( 1 + γ ) / ( 1 − γ ) ) 1 / 2 5\big((1+\gamma)/(1-\gamma)\big)^{1/2} standard deviations of its mean in each coordinate, about 31 31 at γ = 0.95 \gamma=0.95 , so the true laws and their truncations, which the theory covers, coincide for every practical purpose.

sections.heading: Rare-Event Chain.
sections.text: The rare-event chain has d = 2 d=2 , γ = 0.95 \gamma=0.95 and i.i.d. Gaussian per-step rewards with covariance 0.04 ​ 𝐈 0.04\,\mathbf{I} in every channel. At the root, the risky action reaches a bulk channel with mean reward ( 3 , 1 ) (3,1) with probability 1 − p 1-p and a rare channel with mean reward ( − 4 , 2 ) (-4,2) with probability p p , and the safe action reaches a channel with mean reward ( 2.5 , 1.5 ) (2.5,1.5) . The rare channel is adverse in the first coordinate and shifted in the second, so conditional queries on the catastrophe are not trivial. The branching state is preceded by D ∈ { 0 , 2 } D\in\{0,2\} deterministic transient states with reward 0 0 , so for D = 2 D=2 the rare branch is decided two bootstrapping steps below the root, whose return law is γ D \gamma^{D} times that of the branching state. At D = 0 D=0 the return means are ( 60 , 20 ) (60,20) for the bulk, ( − 80 , 40 ) (-80,40) for the rare and ( 50 , 30 ) (50,30) for the safe channel, with standard deviation 0.64 0.64 per coordinate. We use p ∈ { 0.002 , 0.005 , 0.01 } p\in\{0.002,0.005,0.01\} , so p < 1 / M p<1/M already at M = 128 M=128 , and the event Z 1 ≤ − 10 ​ γ D Z_{1}\leq-10\gamma^{D} , between the bulk and the catastrophe. The ground truth is in closed form and agrees with 2 ⋅ 10 5 2\cdot 10^{5} Monte Carlo returns. Every run takes 16 000 16\,000 Bellman steps for D = 0 D=0 and 28 800 28\,800 for D = 2 D=2 , with 50 50 evaluations.

sections.heading: Chain.
sections.text: The chain of Debes and Tuytelaars, 2026b () has K = 10 K=10 reward dimensions, forward probability 0.9 0.9 , γ = 0.9 \gamma=0.9 and the rewards e S ′ + σ r ​ ε e_{S^{\prime}}+\sigma_{r}\varepsilon with σ r ∈ { 0 , 0.05 , 0.2 , 0.5 } \sigma_{r}\in\{0,0.05,0.2,0.5\} . Every method uses M = 128 M=128 particles and near-exact TD targets for 5 ⋅ 10 4 5\cdot 10^{4} updates, and the ground truth uses 10 6 10^{6} Monte Carlo rollouts per start state. The six variants of Debes and Tuytelaars, 2026b () run on their own target sets and on ours, with RAdam at learning rate 2.5 ⋅ 10 − 3 2.5\cdot 10^{-3} , gradient clipping at 0.1 0.1 and 64 64 projections; with more particles, sliced w 2 w_{2} and sliced Cramér at M ∈ { 512 , 2048 , 4096 } M\in\{512,2048,4096\} and MMD at M = 512 M=512 , for σ r ∈ { 0.05 , 0.2 } \sigma_{r}\in\{0.05,0.2\} . SVDRL replaces the cloud by the stratified target set with α = 0.1 \alpha=0.1 and trains the score network of Appendix B alongside.

sections.heading: Resource Gathering.
sections.text: The resource-gathering environment of MO-Gymnasium ( Felten et al.,, 2023 ) is a 5 × 5 5\times 5 grid with d = 3 d=3 , which we reimplement with the attack probability as a parameter, p ∈ { 0.1 , 0.02 , 0.005 } p\in\{0.1,0.02,0.005\} , where the package fixes 0.1 0.1 . We use γ = 0.95 \gamma=0.95 and three fixed policies from value iteration (safe, mixed and risky), and the ground truth comes from exact enumeration. SVDRL runs its single tabular configuration without tuning at M ∈ { 32,128 } M\in\{32,128\} , reported as particles, sampler and hybrid, and the rare-event configuration with N = 10 5 N=10^{5} sampler draws; the particle critics run at M ∈ { 32,128 } M\in\{32,128\} (Sinkhorn at 32 32 only), and a quantile critic on the oracle scalarization with its learning rate tuned on the five tuning seeds. Every run takes 15 680 15\,680 Bellman steps with 50 50 evaluations.

sections.heading: MuJoCo.
sections.text: HalfCheetah, Walker2d, Hopper and Ant (v5) ( Towers et al.,, 2024 ) run for 10 6 10^{6} environment steps with γ = 0.99 \gamma=0.99 and M = 64 M=64 particles, with an evaluation of ten deterministic episodes every 10 4 10^{4} steps. The heads are SAC and SAC with IQN, MD3QN, energy MMD and SVDRL critics on the same trunk. For the critic shape, the policy at 10 6 10^{6} steps is frozen, and 64 64 fixed probes each receive 1000 1000 Monte Carlo rollouts of 1000 1000 steps of the soft return; on Walker2d only the probes that restart exactly are used.

sections.heading: Statistics and Selection.
sections.text: In the tabular experiments and on the chain a seed’s error is its mean over the evaluations in the last 20 % 20\,\% of training (on the chain, the last eight of 40 40 ), and we report the interquartile mean (IQM) or the median over seeds with 95 % 95\,\% percentile-bootstrap intervals. Configurations are selected on tuning seeds and reported on final seeds that the selection did not use: five tuning and ten final seeds for the synthetic MDPs, the chain and resource gathering, and two tuning and ten final seeds for the rare-event study, which adds ten fresh seeds. On the synthetic MDPs and the chain a comparison is a win or a loss when the unpaired Welch t t statistic of SVDRL’s errors against the competitor’s is at most − 2 -2 or at least 2 2 , and a tie otherwise; the best competitor is the row with the lowest seed mean, per MDP, block and framing. In the rare-event study SVDRL is counted as more accurate when its IQM error is smaller than that of the best of the six particle critics at the same M M , answering from its particles or from a Gaussian kernel density estimate on them (Scott’s bandwidth), without a significance test. The three framings of the synthetic MDPs compare SVDRL with the competitors on their own target sets, with every row including the competitors on our target set (marked ∗ ), and with the best competitor at M ∈ { 512 , 4096 } M\in\{512,4096\} on the four unimodal MDPs ( Table 9 ). No competitor is limited by the training budget: on the eight MDPs none improves significantly over the last 20 % 20\,\% of its updates, and SVDRL reaches its plateau early in training. On MuJoCo a run’s return is its mean evaluation return over 800 800 k to 1 1 M steps ( 21 21 evaluations), and we report per environment and head the IQM over five to ten seeds with a 95 % 95\,\% percentile-bootstrap interval; a run stopped by the divergence guard counts with the evaluations it logged.

sections.heading: Metrics.
sections.text: On the synthetic MDPs, mass is the total variation between the mode masses of a cloud and the ground-truth weights, next to its floor min k ⁡ 1 2 ​ ∑ i | k i / M − w i | \min_{k}\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i}|k_{i}/M-w_{i}| over integer allocations k k , and shape is the within-mode error ∑ i w i ​ w 2 2 \sum_{i}w_{i}w_{2}^{2} , in closed form for d = 1 d=1 , by exact assignment against 4096 4096 ground-truth draws for d = 2 d=2 , and by quantile sliced w 2 2 w_{2}^{2} with 128 128 projections for d > 2 d>2 . The full w 2 2 w_{2}^{2} charges a mass error ϵ \epsilon across a gap Δ \Delta as ϵ ​ Δ 2 \epsilon\Delta^{2} , so on separated modes it measures mass rounding rather than shape ( Tables 10 and 6 ). Sliced w 2 w_{2} has two independent estimators, the quantile estimator and a CDF-based estimator that integrates the analytic projected distribution functions of the ground truth ( Vauthier et al.,, 2026 ) , and a disagreement between them fails the asset pipeline. In the rare-event study the queries are CVaR down to α = 0.001 \alpha=0.001 , | log ⁡ P ^ / P | |\log\hat{P}/P| of the event (with a floor of 10 − 6 10^{-6} on P ^ \hat{P} ), chance-constrained decisions over thresholds δ \delta , conditional tails, entropic risk and the expected scalarized return, ten rare-event and two bulk query columns, i.e., 60 60 rare-event and 12 12 bulk comparisons over the six environments. On the chain we measure w 2 w_{2} by exact assignment, sliced and per-coordinate w 2 2 w_{2}^{2} , the mean error and the dispersion against 10 4 10^{4} fresh Monte Carlo rollouts, and the squared energy distance against the 10 6 10^{6} -rollout bank. On resource gathering we measure | log ⁡ P ^ / P | |\log\hat{P}/P| of death, the error rates of the chance-constrained and the CVaR decisions, CVaR errors, the error of 𝔼 ⁡ [ treasure ∣ alive ] \mathds{E}\left[\text{treasure}\mid\text{alive}\right] , the squared energy distance and sliced w 2 2 w_{2}^{2} , and | log ⁡ P ^ / P | |\log\hat{P}/P| of the time-averaged P ^ \hat{P} . On MuJoCo the critic shape is the w 2 w_{2} distance between the critic’s return law and the Monte Carlo law, each centered at its own mean, over the Monte Carlo standard deviation, exact in d = 1 d=1 ; per run we take the median over the two critics and then over the probes, and per environment and head the IQM over seeds with a 5000 5000 -resample bootstrap. Every head’s mean is biased by the twin-critic minimum, so the centered distance is the one that compares the heads. Every evaluation draws fresh randomness, and a size mismatch between a cloud and its reference fails loudly instead of subsampling.

sections.heading: C.1 Compute
sections.text: The Stein move costs at most ( L + 1 ) ​ T ℓ ​ M (L+1)T_{\ell}M score evaluations per state–action pair and update, plus 𝒪 ⁡ ( M 2 ) \mathcal{O}(M^{2}) kernel evaluations per step, independently of the horizon. A sampler run of N N draws costs N ​ N g NN_{\mathrm{g}} score evaluations, vectorized over the draws, and it runs only at evaluation time and inside sampler bootstrapping. Acting takes one forward pass of the critic, which returns the M M Stein particles. Every GPU run used an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090, and training runs in single precision.

Rare-event chain, final seeds. (a) Error of the catastrophe’s probability at the root against p p for D = 2 D=2 , with M = 32 M=32 and M = 128 M=128 , for SVDRL’s variants and the six particle critics: with sampler bootstrapping in the reported configuration (moment-matched, EDM preconditioning) the catastrophe survives the recursion for p ≥ 0.005 p\geq 0.005 , while particle bootstrapping and the particle critics lose it. (b) Errors of the particle critics against their particle count M M at D = 0 D=0 (top) and D = 2 D=2 (bottom), with SVDRL’s sampler at M = 128 M=128 and M = 32 M=32 as horizontal lines: sliced w 2 w_{2} needs about 10 / p = 2048 10/p=2048 particles to resolve the location and the conditional tail of the catastrophe. Figure 5: Return law of the risky root action. In the rare-event chain, a catastrophe of mass p = 0.005 < 1 / M {p=0.005<1/M} lies two steps below the root. (A) Log density of the first coordinate: the true law, the sampler law of ten SVDRL critics and the atoms of ten sliced w 2 w_{2} critics ( M = 128 M=128 ). (B) The catastrophe and (C) the bulk. The sampler gets the probability of the catastrophe right but spreads the rare mode too wide; particles can only hold whole atoms of mass 1 / M 1/M there. Particle critics resolve the catastrophe only with about 10 / p 10/p particles ( Figure 4 b). With M = 2048 M=2048 sliced w 2 w_{2} reaches the CVaR 0.001 error 0.30, below SVDRL’s 6.9, and answers the conditional tail more accurately, while SVDRL keeps the more accurate mass, chance-constrained decisions and bulk ( Section 5 ). SVDRL’s CVaR error at the lowest levels reflects the width of the far rare mode ( Figure 5 ), whose mass the sampler gets right but which the score network spreads too wide, 13 to 15 times in a static fit to draws of the true law ( Appendix E ). The catastrophe survives the recursion only under sampler bootstrapping ( Figure 4 a), as Proposition 6 (v) predicts: a target built from downstream particles gives the catastrophe a multiple of 1 / M 1/M , which is zero for p < 1 / M p<1/M in most updates, whereas a target built from the downstream sampler inherits its event error. At p = 0.002 p=0.002 and M = 32 M=32 the reported configuration loses the catastrophe as well.

sections.heading: D.6 Checks of the Theory
sections.text: We evaluate each bound of Section 4 on the trained networks of MDP1–3, with the ground truth only to measure the left sides ( Tables 19 and 20 ). The checks of the consistency loss add the 3-cycle, a deterministic cycle of three states with rewards 1 1 , − 1 -1 and 0.5 0.5 and γ = 0.9 \gamma=0.9 , whose return laws are point masses. The bound of Theorem 3 holds in 80 of 80 (seed, state–action pair) combinations, but loosely: it exceeds the measured total variation 4.4 to 34 times and the measured w 1 w_{1} by a median factor of 177, the gap between the two being the factor D D of w 1 ≤ D ​ TV w_{1}\leq D\,\mathrm{TV} on the return box. The discretization term is at least 67 % of the bound in every combination, as Remark 2 predicts for the point-mass targets that the particles produce. Several noise levels are necessary ( Remark 2 ). A network trained at the bottom level alone misallocates the mode masses, with errors of 0.32 on MDP2 and 0.46 on MDP3, against 0.056 and 0.099 for the multi-level network trained by DSM alone, and a single level of the order of the mode separation recovers the masses on MDP3 but not on MDP2. Sampler bootstrapping without moment matching accumulates the smoothing of the sampler over the horizon ( Remark 5 ), and moment matching removes the accumulation: with it, sampler bootstrapping and sampler-seeded particles match the Stein particles on MDP1–3 in w ¯ 1 \bar{w}_{1} and in the mode masses, all differences within their intervals ( Table 19 ). The level-by-level bound of Corollary 3 holds at every level in 87 of 87 seeds ( Table 20 ). On the stochastic MDP1, consistency-only training with a lagged target reaches a lower multi-level risk than DSM alone, as Lemmas 5 and 1 predict, and with the online network as its own target it diverges on the self-looping state–action pair, which is the lag condition after Corollary 4 . sections.heading: Appendix E Limitations in Detail
sections.text: SVDRL is not the most accurate critic on every return law, and this section collects the evidence for the limits of Section 7 . The sampler fails on atomic and widely separated laws, on the atomic chain ( Section D.3 ) and on resource gathering ( Section D.4 ), as Lemma 2 predicts, and the hybrid rule reports the particles there. At equal size or matched compute, fitted particle clouds beat SVDRL’s sampler on the unimodal MDPs and on the chain with reward noise ( Tables 9 and 8 ). The measured gap ε St \varepsilon_{\mathrm{St}} is undefined for the rare-event configuration, which keeps no particles, and on separated modes it flags a disagreement but can exceed both errors ( Table 12 ). In SAC-SVDRL the linear variance of the moment head reached its floor and made one Ant seed diverge, a floor that a log-variance head cannot reach ( Section D.5 ), and we make no claim about a sampler on MuJoCo. A light rare mode far from the bulk comes out too wide, an extrapolation limit of the score network where the data are sparse. A static fit of the selected score network to fixed draws of the true root law of the rare-event chain, without bootstrapping, consistency loss or EMA, reproduces the width, with a standard deviation of the rare component 13 to 15 times the true one ( Table 21 ). sections.heading: E.1 Pixel Maze
sections.text: On the maze of Zhang et al., (2021) under the pixel protocol of Debes and Tuytelaars, 2026b () , the competitors’ benchmark from pixels, SVDRL is third of four heads in every variant ( Table 22 ). The benchmark evaluates the uniform random policy from pixels with a PQN backbone in three variants, and every head is compared with Monte Carlo returns at the start state; SVDRL runs there without the consistency loss ( Table 4 ). In SVDRL’s first configuration nothing that trained the trunk depended on the transition, so the trunk was blind to the state and the action. Taking the moment-matching mean from each transition’s bootstrap targets, as on Walker2d, Hopper and Ant, together with the log-variance moment head, removes this blindness and improves SVDRL in two of three variants, but it stays behind the sliced Cramér and multiquadric MMD critics. sections.heading: E.2 Multi-Objective MuJoCo
sections.text: The standardization by the moment head limits SAC-SVDRL in distributional policy evaluation of fixed policies on mo-halfcheetah and mo-hopper ( Table 23 ). With its selected configuration, SVDRL’s particles lie between MD3QN and energy MMD in energy distance after 10 6 10^{6} steps on both environments, and behind both after 5 ⋅ 10 5 5\cdot 10^{5} steps. The remaining gap is under-dispersion: the EMA target cloud is narrower than the online one, which the bootstrap compounds by up to the factor 1 / ( 1 − γ 2 ) 1/(1-\gamma^{2}) , about 50 50 at γ = 0.99 \gamma=0.99 . The sampler of the selected configuration fails its ground-truth-free gate on three of four policies. A float32 cancellation in PopArt’s variance accumulator affected the low-coefficient-of-variation targets of the first multi-objective runs. We reran the HalfCheetah baselines with a centered accumulator, and these rows, together with SVDRL’s selected configuration, which uses it, are the comparison there; the uncentered HalfCheetah rows are kept for reference. Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2610.17925v1 [cs.LG] 13 Oct 2026 Stein Variational Distributional Reinforcement Learning: Score-Guided Particles for Multivariate Return Distributions Abstract Decisions that weigh several reward signals against each other require the joint distribution of the return vector. Categorical critics scale exponentially in the reward dimension, and quantiles have no canonical multivariate analogue. Multivariate distributional critics therefore represent each return distribution by M M equal-weight particles trained with a discrepancy loss. Beyond their atoms, the particles provide no sampler and cannot resolve events rarer than 1 / M 1/M . We propose Stein variational distributional RL (SVDRL). Its critic outputs Stein particles, which Stein variational gradient descent transports along a learned score field of the distributional Bellman target. We learn this field by bootstrapped denoising score matching across noise levels and tie it across the Bellman recursion by a consistency loss, which we prove is a non-expansive temporal-difference scheme in score space. The same field certifies the particles. Its reverse-diffusion sampler satisfies a supremal Wasserstein policy-evaluation bound that holds for bounded, possibly multimodal returns. The Stein particles inherit this bound up to a gap that we measure without ground truth, and the sampler answers tail-risk queries below the particle resolution at any sample size. Empirically, SVDRL is more accurate on rare events than particle critics with the same number of particles, and on par on MuJoCo continuous control. Stein Variational Distributional Reinforcement Learning: Score-Guided Particles for Multivariate Return Distributions Manuel Haußmann Melih Kandemir University of Southern Denmark 1 Introduction Distributional reinforcement learning models the distribution of the return rather than only its expectation ( Bellemare et al.,, 2017 ) . With multivariate rewards, risk- and correlation-sensitive decisions depend on the joint distribution of the return components ( Zhang et al.,, 2021 ; Hayes et al.,, 2022 ) . The univariate representations do not carry over: categorical grids ( Bellemare et al.,, 2017 ) need 𝒪 ⁡ ( M d ) \mathcal{O}(M^{d}) atoms, and quantiles ( Dabney et al., 2018a, ; Dabney et al., 2018b, ) have no canonical analogue for d > 1 d>1 . Existing multivariate methods therefore represent the return distribution by M M particles trained with a discrepancy loss, e.g., MMD ( Zhang et al.,, 2021 ) , Sinkhorn divergences ( Sun et al.,, 2024 ) , or sliced divergences ( Debes and Tuytelaars, 2026b, ) . The theory of these methods covers the Bellman operator, which contracts in the respective supremal divergence, but not the learned particles. We show that this gap is structural. Equal-weight particles carry no density and no sampler, and M M of them cannot represent an event of probability below 1 / M 1/M , whatever loss trains them ( Propositions 1 and 1 ). We instead learn the return score field , the smoothed score of the return distribution at all noise levels. Smoothing commutes with the Bellman update up to a rescaling of the noise level ( Lemma 1 ), so the field satisfies its own Bellman equation, and we learn it along a noise schedule ( Song and Ermon,, 2019 ) by bootstrapped denoising score matching ( Lemma 4 ) and by temporal differences in score space ( Theorem 2 ). A single noise level does not suffice, as it cannot certify mode masses ( Remark 2 ). We sample from the field by reverse diffusion. For fast action selection we additionally keep M M particles per state–action pair, the Stein particles, which we transport along the field by Stein variational gradient descent (SVGD) ( Liu and Wang,, 2016 ) and amortize into a critic. The training risk controls the sampled return distribution in total variation and w 1 w_{1} for bounded multimodal returns, where log-concavity and related assumptions fail ( Theorem 3 ). This yields a policy-evaluation bound in w ¯ 1  ar{w}_{1} ( Theorem 4 ), certified mode masses ( Corollaries 6 and 8 ), and a CVaR estimate whose error does not depend on M M ( Theorem 6 ). No single critic is accurate on every return law, and we show which error limits each family. Equal-weight particles suffer from a resolution floor : they round event probabilities and mixture weights to multiples of 1 / M 1/M ( Proposition 1 ). A score field suffers from smoothing bias and is hard to learn where the return law is atomic or its modes lie far apart relative to their widths ( Propositions 2 and 2 ). SVDRL keeps both objects, and a hybrid rule reports, per state–action pair and without ground truth, the Stein particles on separated or atomic clusters and the sampler draws elsewhere ( Definitions 1 and 1 ). SVDRL is, to our knowledge, the first certified multivariate score-based critic for possibly multimodal returns, and its Stein particles inherit the certificate up to a gap measured without ground truth ( Theorem 4 ). At equal particle count, SVDRL is more accurate than the best particle critic in every rare-event comparison ( Section 5 ). On all eight synthetic MDPs the hybrid wins within-mode shape against the competitors as specified, although at matched compute they win the unimodal ones. The competitors’ own benchmarks place the boundary at atomic laws, and on MuJoCo SAC-SVDRL is on par in return and has the most accurate critic distribution on three of four. Its stratified Bellman target set and running-mean moment matching improve every particle critic we tested. Figure 1: A rare event below the particle resolution. Schematic. A catastrophe of mass p < 1 / M p<1/M needs a fraction of a particle, so particle critics round its probability to a multiple of 1 / M 1/M ( Proposition 1 ). SVDRL learns a density, which carries any mass; on the rare-event chain it estimates p = 0.005 p=0.005 far better than particle critics with M = 128 M=128 ( Sections 5 and 5 ). 2 Background and Notation Markov Decision Processes with Multivariate Rewards. In the tabular experiments a seed’s error is its mean over the last 20 % 20\,\% of training, which averages out the fluctuation of single evaluations. Configurations are selected on tuning seeds and reported on different seeds that the selection did not use, in the rare-event study additionally on a second set of fresh seeds. We report the interquartile mean (IQM) or median over seeds with 95 % 95\,\% bootstrap intervals; on the synthetic MDPs and the chain a comparison is a win or a loss when the Welch t t statistic is at most − 2 -2 or at least 2 2 , and in the rare-event study it compares IQM errors ( Appendix C ). The particle competitors are MMD critics ( Nguyen-Tang et al.,, 2021 ; Zhang et al.,, 2021 ) with RBF, MD3QN and energy kernels, sliced Cramér and sliced w 2 w_{2} critics, the persistent-particle objectives of Debes and Tuytelaars, 2026b () and Sinkhorn critics ( Sun et al.,, 2024 ) , each with a tuned learning rate and each also run with our stratified target set ( Section B.1 ).
